irrigation-s1.title: Water used by four irrigation methods

table.caption: One season of the same crop on 1 hectare of the same soil (invented data for practice)
cols: Water taken up by the crop (m³ per ha)

irrigation-s2.title: Depth to groundwater in a farm well

plot.label: Line graph of the depth from the surface down to the water table in a farm well, every ten years from 1980 to 2020, invented data

items.q: Which irrigation method delivers water slowly through tubes to the base of each plant?
options: Drip irrigation
Furrow irrigation
Flood irrigation
Spray irrigation

why.correct: Drip irrigation runs tubes with small holes along the rows, so water goes straight to the roots.
options: Right: drip puts water at the roots.
Furrow irrigation runs water down trenches between rows.
Flood irrigation covers the whole field.
Spray irrigation sprinkles water over the crop from above.

items.q: Why is drip irrigation more efficient than furrow irrigation?
options: Water goes to the roots, so less evaporates from the surface or runs off the field
Drip water contains more nutrients, so the plants need less of it to grow
Drip tubes cool the soil around the roots, so plants take up water at a slower rate
Drip systems pump water faster, so it reaches the roots before evaporating

why.correct: Efficiency is the share of water applied that the crop uses. Drip loses little to evaporation and runoff because it wets only the soil around each plant.
options: Right: little water is lost before it reaches the roots.
The water is the same; the difference is where it goes.
Drip does not work by cooling the soil.
Drip delivers water slowly, not fast.

items.q: A farmer in a poor region is choosing an irrigation method. Which is the main drawback of drip irrigation for this farmer?
options: It costs the most to buy and install
It wastes the most water of the four methods
It is the most likely to cause waterlogging
It needs the field to be covered with water

why.correct: Drip irrigation saves water, but its tubing and fittings are expensive to install and maintain.
options: Right: high cost is drip's main drawback.
Drip wastes the least water.
Drip applies small amounts, so it rarely waterlogs soil.
That describes flood irrigation.

items.q: How does irrigation with fresh river water lead to salinization of farmland?
options: River water carries a little dissolved salt, and evaporation leaves the salt behind in the soil
River water slowly turns into salt water as it soaks down through the layers of the soil
Fertilizer added to the river water is changed into table salt by bacteria in the soil
Plant roots release salt into the soil whenever they take up river water

why.correct: Fresh water is not pure. When irrigation water evaporates, only the water leaves; the salt accumulates over many seasons.
options: Right: evaporation leaves the dissolved salt behind.
Water does not turn into salt water in the soil.
Bacteria do not make table salt from fertilizer.
Roots take up water and leave most salt behind; they do not release salt.

items.q: A field that is irrigated too heavily becomes waterlogged. Why do the crops suffer?
options: Water fills the pore spaces, so roots cannot get the oxygen they need
The extra water dissolves the roots, so plants are unable to take up water
Waterlogged soil is too dry at the surface for the seeds to germinate
Waterlogged soil heats up, so the roots are damaged by the warm temperature

why.correct: Roots need oxygen from air in the soil pores. When water fills every pore, roots suffocate.
options: Right: no air in the pores means no oxygen for roots.
Water does not dissolve roots.
Waterlogged soil is wet, not dry.
The harm comes from a lack of oxygen, not heat.

items.q: In parts of the Great Plains, farmers pump water from the Ogallala Aquifer faster than rain refills it. What is the most likely long-term result?
options: The water table falls, wells must be drilled deeper, and some farms switch back to dryland crops
The water table rises, so the soil above the aquifer becomes waterlogged over large areas
The aquifer refills faster to match the extra pumping, so the water table stays at the same depth
The water in the aquifer turns salty, so it can be used just for watering livestock

why.correct: Withdrawal greater than recharge depletes the aquifer: the water table drops and pumping costs rise until some wells fail.
options: Right: depletion lowers the water table and raises pumping costs.
Overpumping lowers the water table; it does not raise it.
Recharge depends on rain and snowmelt, not on how fast farmers pump.
The main result of overpumping an inland aquifer like this is a falling water table.

items.q: A farmer applies 25 mm of water to a 40-hectare field. How many cubic meters of water is that? (1 ha = 10,000 m²; 1,000 mm = 1 m)

mistakes.why: The depth is in millimeters. Change 25 mm to 0.025 m before multiplying by the area in square meters.
The area is in hectares. Change 40 ha to 400,000 m² so the units multiply to cubic meters.

items.q: Water costs 0.15 dollars per cubic meter. Write the setup for the cost of 10,000 m³ of irrigation water, then give the answer. (Type the answer as a number followed by "dollars".)

why.correct: Multiply so the cubic meters cancel: $10{,}000\,\text{m}^3 \times \frac{0.15\,\text{dollars}}{1\,\text{m}^3} = 1{,}500$ dollars.

mistakes.why: Price per cubic meter times cubic meters gives dollars. Multiply; dividing gives cubic meters per dollar.
Multiply the volume by the price per cubic meter so the cubic meters cancel.
A factor of 10 slipped: 10,000 × 0.15 = 1,500.
A factor of 10 slipped the other way: 0.15 is fifteen hundredths, so 10,000 × 0.15 = 1,500.

items.q: Which method in the table delivered the most water that the crop did not take up?
options: Flood, with 5,200 m³ per ha not taken up
Furrow, with 2,700 m³ per ha not taken up
Spray, with 1,200 m³ per ha not taken up
Drip, with 400 m³ per ha not taken up

why.correct: Applied minus taken up: flood $10{,}000 - 4{,}800 = 5{,}200$; furrow 2,700; spray 1,200; drip 400 m³ per ha.
options: Right: flood lost 5,200 m³ per ha.
Furrow lost 2,700, less than flood.
Spray lost 1,200.
Drip lost the least, 400.

items.q: Write the setup for the efficiency of furrow irrigation (the percent of water applied that the crop takes up), then give the answer.

mistakes.why: Efficiency puts the useful part (water the crop takes up, 4,800) on top and the total applied (7,500) on the bottom.
That is the fraction. Multiply by 100 to give a percent.
36% is the share lost (2,700 of 7,500). Efficiency is the share the crop takes up.
0.64 is the fraction. Multiply by 100 for the percent.

items.q: Write the setup for the percent change in water applied when a farm switches from flood to drip irrigation, then give the answer.

why.correct: $\frac{5{,}000 - 10{,}000}{10{,}000} \times 100 = -50\%$: drip uses half as much water.

mistakes.why: Divide by the starting value, the 10,000 m³ used by flood irrigation.
Subtract old from new: (5,000 - 10,000). Water use fell, so the change is negative.
That is the change from drip back to flood. Start from flood, the old method.
Water use fell, so the percent change is negative: -50%.

items.q: A 50-hectare farm switches from flood to spray irrigation. Using the table, how many cubic meters of water does it save in one season?

why.correct: Saving per hectare: $10{,}000 - 6{,}000 = 4{,}000$ m³/ha. For the farm: $4{,}000\,\frac{\text{m}^3}{\text{ha}} \times 50\,\text{ha} = 200{,}000\,\text{m}^3$.

mistakes.why: 4,000 m³ is the saving for one hectare. Multiply by the 50 hectares.
That is the water spray irrigation uses. The saving is the difference, (10,000 - 6,000) × 50.

items.q: Using the cost column, which statement best explains why many farmers keep using flood or furrow irrigation?
options: They cost far less to install, so farmers who pay little for water save money
They waste less water than the others, so farmers save on both water and equipment
They let crops take up more water, so the crops grow faster than with drip
They use the newest equipment, so they are easier to repair than drip

why.correct: Flood costs 150 dollars per ha to install and drip 3,200. Where water is cheap, the water savings may not pay back the equipment.
options: Right: low cost to install is their main advantage.
They waste more water, not less.
The crop took up 4,800 m³ under flood and furrow, about the same as under the other methods.
Flood and furrow use simple ditches, not new equipment.
The water table got deeper by about 9 m each decade
The water table rose toward the surface by about 9 m each decade
The water table stayed near 15 m below the surface from 1980 to 2020
The water table fell quickly at first, then leveled off after 2000

why.correct: Depth rose from 15 m to 51 m in steps of 9 m per decade, so the water table moved steadily down.
options: Right: depth increased by 9 m each decade.
A larger depth means the water is farther down, not rising.
The depth changed from 15 to 51 m.
The change was steady, 9 m each decade.

items.q: At what average rate did the water table drop from 1980 to 2020, in meters per year?

mistakes.why: That uses one decade. The drop of 36 m happened over 40 years, from 1980 to 2020.
36 m is the total drop. Divide by the 40 years for a rate per year.

items.q: The well's pump sits 78 m below the surface. If the water table keeps falling at the same rate after 2020, in what year will it reach the pump?

why.correct: Distance left: $78 - 51 = 27$ m. Time: $\frac{27\,\text{m}}{0.9\,\text{m/yr}} = 30$ years. Year: $2020 + 30 = 2050$.

mistakes.why: 30 is the number of years. The question asks for the year: add it to 2020.
The water table is already 51 m down. Use the distance left, 78 - 51 = 27 m.

items.q: Propose a solution a farmer could use to slow the drop shown in the graph, and explain how it works.

why.correct: A solution fitted to one farm, with its mechanism: switching from flood or furrow to drip irrigation puts water only at the roots, so less is lost and less must be pumped.

solution.label: Solution
options: switch from flood to drip irrigation
drill the well deeper
plant a crop that needs more water

why.1: A deeper well reaches the water but pumps it out faster; it does not slow the drop.
why.2: A thirstier crop needs more pumping.

mechanism.label: How it works
options: delivers water only to the roots, so less is lost to evaporation and runoff
adds water back to the aquifer from the river
raises the price of water for the neighbors

why.1: Drip irrigation does not recharge an aquifer.
why.2: Drip irrigation does not change what neighbors pay.

effect.label: Result
options: less groundwater is pumped each season and the water table falls more slowly
the water table rises above the surface
the crop takes up less water and dies

why.1: Saving water slows the drop; it will not lift the water table above the ground.
why.2: The crop gets about the same water; less is wasted.

specific.model: The farmer could switch from flood to drip irrigation, which delivers water only to the roots and reduces the water lost to evaporation and runoff. As a result less groundwater is pumped each season and the water table falls more slowly.
